narration: And according to the Park Service, a family dog named Darkey once rode that wire two thousand feet down the mountain.

intent: visitors stand before a huge painting of a red canyon in a grand gallery
narration: He painted it. His canvases of Zion were shown at the nineteen oh four World's Fair in St. Louis, and he wrote about the canyon for Scribner's Magazine, calling it a new valley of wonders.

intent: a steam locomotive pulls a long passenger train across the desert
narration: In June nineteen twenty-three, the biggest tourist of all arrived. President Warren Harding came to Cedar City, Utah, by train, to thousands of cheering locals. Sheriffs rounded up about seventy-five horses to ride him up the canyon. According to a Deseret News account, the president wore a cowboy hat, a kerchief and a pair of oversized chaps. His wife, Florence, said she wouldn't have missed the trip for anything.

intent: a surveyor with a brass instrument on a tripod at a rock ledge facing red canyon cliffs
narration: It took more than four years of surveys just to find a route. A local stockman, John Winder, is credited with showing the surveyors the way up Pine Creek. When they were done, the road to Bryce Canyon would shrink from a hundred and forty-nine miles to eighty-eight.

intent: inside a tunnel under construction a drill rig, work lamps and a dynamite blast flash at the far end, silhouetted workers
narration: The crews started by blasting openings in the cliff face, windows high above Pine Creek. Through them, they hauled out the rock and let in air and light. Then they bored the tunnel in two directions, toward each other, and widened it with dynamite and air shovels. Several times, parts of it collapsed.

narration: Construction began in September nineteen twenty-seven. A Nevada construction company from Fallon took the job. About two hundred workers and their families lived in a camp near the work.

intent: a rock tunnel with a window in the cliff wall letting a shaft of light onto the road, rubble blocking part of it, a dry leaf
era: present day, a sealed gallery window
narration: Not everything has lasted. One of the windows was closed because seepage turned the road to ice. Another was sealed by a rockslide in nineteen fifty-eight, and two more were closed later. The same mountain that the tunnel crosses keeps working on it, which is the same story as the lakebed, the lodge and the trail: this canyon is always moving.
